doc.title: Junior Mance Part I interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, New York City, New York, July 27, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Not liking his own records; first album Junior with Ray Brown
summary: Self-criticism, and his first Verve album as leader with Ray Brown and Lex Humphries.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography

blocks.x: Do you have a favorite record of your own?
That’s one of my secret ambitions is to make a record that I like.
Make a record you like? Oh!
Do you think you’re overly critical?
With myself? I could be. That’s what everybody says. But I don’t know why I’m like that. I listen to my records like in the studio and I may listen to like the rough draft of it,

like when they give you the cassettes to take home. But when it comes out I never listen to it. I may hear it by accident like on WBGO you know, the jazz station, or something like that. But I don’t play them at home. I never listen to them. I know, when you said about being overly critical, I think I might be because I used to always, I remember when I first started recording I would say now why did I do that? Why didn’t I do such-and- such a thing? The only record I really liked that I ever made was my first album as a leader. After that I don’t know, I just didn’t like them. My first one was on Verve, it’s a record called “Junior.” I was playing with Dizzy at the time and Norman Granz was the producer of it. And Dizzy was also with Verve. He produced Dizzy’s album and then we had just done two albums. So Norman, he liked the way I played and he asked me he says, “How would you like to make a record?” I said, “Yeah, of course.” He says, “Do you mind using Ray Brown?” I says [stammers]. We had a great bass player too, Sam Jones was the bass player that Dizzy really loved and who I was going to use anyway. But Ray, he was like, he was the big man then, and I used Dizzy’s drummer, a youngster, this guy was only like nineteen years old, named Lex Humphries. He was the drummer. And I enjoyed doing that album, because Norman was there, and the first couple of things we did, it went down in one take. So Norman was kind of tired that day because he had been doing a million other, I think he’d been recording some of the other people that recorded on Verve then. And he said, “Well you guys don’t really need me.” He says, “You can finish by yourself.” So it was just the three of us and the engineer. And I enjoyed what I did. You know the engineer would listen to it and he said, “Well you like that? Are you satisfied with that?” And Ray was very helpful. Ray was saying, “Sounds good to me.” Ray wouldn’t even play solos, you know, I forced him into playing a solo on one of them, a slow blues, and while we were playing I just stopped and pointed to Ray. And it was such a good take at that point, so he had to take a couple of choruses you know. But the reason he didn’t play, he says, “This is your date, this is your first one, you’re the star here.”
